newsitem.title: FRANCE: French unions renew protests, but on small scale.
newsitem.headline: French unions renew protests, but on small scale.

text.p: French workers renewed street protests on Saturday against unpopular government welfare reforms, but in much smaller numbers than their trade union leaders had hoped.

In the southern port city of Marseille, just 3,000 people showed up to march, according to police, although organisers said the number was closer to 10,000. In Toulouse, southern France, just 2,500 to 3,500 demonstrated, police and organisers said.
Saturday's demonstrations were called to coincide with the first anniversary of a controversial welfare reform plan unveiled by conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe on November 15, 1995.

Juppe's approval rating hit a record low of 25 percent this week in a Gallup poll for the weekly L'Express, but protests were far smaller than last year, when crippling transport and public sector strikes virtually paralysed France for more than three weeks in November and December.

Despite the low protest turn-out, the leader of the Communist-led CGT union pledged to organise a further day of national action in coming weeks in protest against government austerity policies during a time of record unemployment.
CGT secretary general Louis Viannet said new demonstrations across France were needed due to "a system which is leading to more and more pressure on our finances".
He spoke a day after a public transport strike called for Paris failed to materialise.

Transport union leaders had hoped that Friday's strike would paralyse the capital and thus crown a week of protests in favour of wage increases and against job cuts and privatisations with unemployment at 12.6 percent in September.
But city transport officials said Paris commuter services ran at near-normal levels throughout the day as union members failed to heed their leaders' call for action.

However a strike by pilots' unions at Air France Europe, part of the Air France group, entered its second and final day on Saturday and succeeded in grounding half of the carrier's scheduled flights, airline officials said.
The 48-hour strike called by the USPNT, SPIT, SNPNAC and SPNL unions was intended to protest at planned job cuts.
